analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from collecting, selling, or keeping personal data of children and teens.
analysis.headline: The bill passed its first House subcommittee by voice vote in December 2025 and now awaits action by the full Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for data brokers—companies that buy and resell people's personal information—to collect, sell, or keep the personal data of anyone under 18 that they know about. Brokers would have to delete what they already hold, honor deletion requests from teens or parents within 10 days, and face enforcement by the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with cash penalties of at least $1,000 per violation. It takes effect 180 days after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers under 18, whose personal information could no longer be bought, sold, or traded by data brokers without their consent, and parents, who could demand deletion of their child's data within 10 days. All internet users indirectly benefit from shrinking the market for kids' profiles that can be exploited for fraud, stalking, or targeted manipulation.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from collecting, using, maintaining, or selling any personal data of an individual they know is a child (under 13) or teen (13 to 17), and requires deletion of data they already hold [S2].

Requires data brokers to honor deletion requests submitted by teens, parents, or guardians within 10 days and to notify the requester when done, with a plainly written public notice of the process [S2].

Gives the FTC enforcement power, allows state attorneys general to sue on behalf of residents, and lets individuals sue with damages of at least $1,000 per violation, tripled for willful violations, plus attorney fees—rights that cannot be waived by terms of service or forced into arbitration [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the online advertising ecosystem built on reselling personal information would lose access to a market of users under 18 and bear compliance costs for deletion systems, plus FTC, state, and private enforcement exposure. Some websites and apps that rely on broker-fed advertising revenue could earn less from younger users.

drawbacks.text: The ban only applies to data of children and teens the broker 'knows' is a minor, based on actual knowledge or what circumstances fairly imply—brokers holding data without age signals could claim they did not know, a gap that limits how much protection the bill delivers in practice [S2].

The bill defines 'data broker' narrowly and exempts service providers and companies for which data is not the product, so many platforms and ad-tech intermediaries that collect children's data directly are outside its reach [S2].

Minimum statutory damages of $1,000 per violation, trebled for willful violations, could generate high-volume litigation costs for companies, a cost that some critics argue gets passed to consumers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—removing minors' personal data from a market where it is bought and sold—is substantial for families and carries little direct cost to ordinary people. The bill's main weaknesses are enforcement-shaped rather than cost-shaped: the knowledge standard and narrow broker definition leave loopholes that large platforms and intermediaries may exploit. The compliance and litigation costs fall on the data-broker industry, which is the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee markup by voice vote in December 2025 and is waiting for the full Energy and Commerce Committee to take it up before it can reach the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ), the top Democrat on the Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on November 25, 2025, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee [S1][S4].
On December 11, 2025, the subcommittee held a markup session and forwarded the bill to the full committee in the nature of a substitute (amended) by voice vote [S4].
The bill has no cosponsors as of the record [S3].
The bill has not yet been considered by the full committee or received a vote in either chamber, and the 119th Congress remains in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet; the bill is still alive in committee. Data brokers continue operating under current rules in the meantime.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: Ranking Member (top Democrat), House Energy and Commerce Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Don't Sell Kids' Data Act on November 25, 2025, a bill banning data brokers from collecting or selling minors' personal data.

for.name: Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee (House Energy and Commerce)
for.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the bill
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on December 11, 2025, and forwarded the bill to the full committee, amended, by voice vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and no floor votes have occurred, so the partisan shape is not yet visible in the record [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill directly targets their core business: buying, holding, and reselling personal data. They would have to delete all known minors' data, build deletion-request systems, and face FTC, state, and private suits with $1,000-per-violation minimum damages [S2].

The bill is narrower than it first appears—companies collecting data directly from users are exempt from the 'data broker' definition, and the knowledge standard lets firms avoid liability where age is not apparent [S2]. Still, the ad ecosystem loses access to broker-sourced profiles of minors that help target ads.

analysis.trajectory: The bill's subcommittee passage by voice vote is a modest positive sign, but a single sponsor with zero cosponsors, referral to the minority party's chairman's committee, and no full-committee action yet mean the usual path for a first-term privacy bill is a hearing and possible further markup if the committee prioritizes it—floor action is unlikely unless leadership elevates kids' online privacy this Congress.
